title: Why Some People Read the Ending First
desc: Have you ever peeked at the last page and enjoyed the story anyway? We'll explore a surprising experiment about spoilers, how knowing the ending can make a story easier to follow, and why other research found a different result. Settle in, get comfortable, and let's follow the clues together.

plan: b01: Open A03/living_room_day with the gentle last-page moment: you know the ending, yet keep reading; within 15 seconds introduce the question of whether surprise is essential to enjoyment, then an unnumbered list titled 'Tonight, we'll explore'. Introduce Leavitt and Christenfeld's UC San Diego paper, published in 2011, as the central F04 study; explain its short-story comparison and pay off the opening question with higher average enjoyment for externally spoiled stories. Set and resolve a local loop about whether mysteries followed the same pattern; hand over the larger question of why spoiler placement mattered.

b02: Open A10/bedroom_night and reconstruct the central study's design: each participant read an unaltered story, a story preceded by an external spoiler, and a story with the spoiler incorporated into its opening; explain counterbalancing and enjoyment ratings. Pay off the placement loop: external spoilers improved enjoyment, while incorporated spoilers showed no significant benefit. Use the mystery ratings 7.29 versus 6.60 on a list card, preserving decimals; distinguish rated enjoyment from memory or comprehension. Set and pay off why the comparison used different readers rather than asking someone to experience one ending as unknown twice; bridge to the possible mechanism.

b03: Open A13/living_room_day and explore processing fluency: knowing the destination may help you interpret the clues along the way. Use Leavitt and Christenfeld's UC San Diego follow-up, published in 2013, which measured pleasure midway through stories and reported mediation by processing fluency. Set and pay off whether any benefit had to wait until the final page: it appeared before the ending. Explain the differing results for very easy stories and spoiler simplicity without inventing effect sizes; identify fluency as a supported explanation in these experiments, not a diagnosis of people who seek spoilers. Bridge to whether the original benefit holds across studies.

b04: Open A19/bedroom_night and examine the central study's limits: short stories, a university subject pool, average ratings, and externally supplied spoilers do not establish why an individual chooses the last page. Contrast Johnson and Rosenbaum's 412-participant study, first published online in 2014 and appearing in a 2015 issue, which found unspoiled stories more fun, suspenseful, moving, and enjoyable overall. Set and pay off the apparent contradiction by distinguishing measures and study conditions; present mixed findings without claiming those differences conclusively explain them. Bridge from a universal rule to choosing the experience you personally enjoy.

b05: Open A01/living_room_day with takeaways grounded in the central experiment and its limitations: knowing an ending can coexist with enjoyment, surprise is one ingredient, and average results cannot prescribe your preference. Set and pay off whether knowing the destination leaves anything to discover: return to the supported fluency explanation and the experience of following how events unfold. Suggest an optional personal comparison using different unfamiliar short stories, explicitly as reflection rather than a scientific test, and ask before sharing an ending with someone else. Call back to the opening last-page moment, then guide a gentle wind-down using a closed book and a quiet room; break char runs with list, quote, and photo scenes. Finish with an end segment teasing a future exploration of why familiar places can feel different after time away.
